role.altitude: The sawyer keeps running and adjusting the saw, clearing jams safely, grading boards and choosing blades and stock; counting pieces, writing tallies and fetching paper work orders shrink.
skills_to_grow: Coding stoppage causes on the line terminal consistently
role.ambitious_version: A sawyer who sees the next order and its stock location before the current pack is done.

tasks.short: Monitor sawing machines by sight and sound, adjust speed and tension, stop the line and clear jams safely, and note stoppages with their causes.

steps.what: Sawyer monitors the sawing machines by watching the line and listening for problems
Sawyer adjusts feed speed and blade tension
Sawyer stops the line, locks it out and clears jams
Sawyer records stoppages and their causes: on the shift sheet today; after the change the controller logs stop times on saws that have one and the sawyer enters each cause on the line terminal

tasks.design: Running, adjusting and clearing jams stay fully with the sawyer, and lockout stays a manual safety step; no software takes part in any safety function. The only change: the saw's controller logs every stop with its start and end time, and the sawyer taps the cause on the line terminal instead of writing the shift sheet.
tasks.previous_blocker: Stoppages were written up from memory at the end of the shift.
tasks.enabler_now: Machine controllers that log stops and line terminals with cause lists.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing a blade start to wander before it ruins a board.

reach.learn: Whether stop causes point to recurring faults.

evidence.claim: Machine controllers log stop times that a line terminal can show for cause coding.
Stop logs per operator could monitor performance and need works council consent if used that way.

assumptions: Boundary: running the saw during a shift; maintenance is outside.
Input contract for s4: stop start and end times logged by the saw's controller on saws that have one (about 60%); older saws keep the paper sheet; s4 is priced at that share.

Monitoring, adjusting and clearing jams keep their full time. s4 keeps 70: on older saws the sheet stays, and on saws with a controller only writing the times goes while the cause is still the sawyer's own entry.
unknowns: Which saws have a controller that logs stops.
research_questions: Do stop records become more complete?

incremental.description: Sawyer suggests changes to the cause list.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: only about a third of the saws have a controller that logs stops, so most stop times are still written (1.3); high: about 60% of saws log stops as assumed (2.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Sort boards by grade and length, stack finished workpieces for drying or shipping, count pieces per pack and write the pack tally and label.

steps.what: Sawyer sorts finished boards by grade and length
Sawyer stacks finished workpieces in packs with sticks for drying or shipping
Sawyer counts the pieces in each pack
Sawyer prepares the pack tally and label: count, dimensions and grade written on a paper label today; after the change shown on the line terminal from the counter and the work order
Sawyer checks the pack before closing it: count, dimensions and grade on the terminal against the pack on the line
Sawyer closes the checked pack on the line terminal, which prints its label

tasks.design: A photo-eye counter at the outfeed counts the pieces going into each pack, and the sawyer checks the pack on the line terminal and closes it once, which prints a label with the actual count and the dimensions and grade from the work order. Length sorting follows the bin settings on lines with a sorting conveyor; grading by eye and stacking stay with the sawyer. Buying a mechanical stacker is a separate capital decision outside this design.

approvals.approved_version: The pack record with piece count, dimensions and grade exactly as checked by the sawyer in s4b, closed once on the line terminal and printed on the label for that pack; any change needs a new check and a new label.

tasks.previous_blocker: Pieces were counted by hand and tallies written on paper labels.
tasks.enabler_now: Outfeed counters and label printers linked to work orders.
tasks.still_hard: Grading boards with knots and wane.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing a board that will warp in the kiln.
tasks.altitude: Less counting and writing; the physical work stays.

reach.learn: Whether printed labels cut packs with wrong counts.

evidence.claim: Photo-eye counters count pieces at a conveyor outfeed and can feed a label printer.
No AI is used; counting and labelling are fixed logic.

assumptions: Boundary: from sawn boards to labelled packs; drying and shipping are outside.
Input contract for s3: piece counts from the outfeed counter on lines that have one (about 70%); other lines are counted by hand; s3 is priced at that share.
Input contract for s4: the actual count from s3 and the work order's dimensions and grade, shown on the line terminal from production planning.

Sorting and stacking keep their full or nearly full time; s1 keeps 85 because length sorting follows bin settings on lines with a sorting conveyor. s3 keeps 35 for hand counts on lines without a counter; s4 keeps 45 for reading the tally and for hand-counted lines; the check and the close keep their full time.
research_questions: Do count disputes with customers fall?

already_counted.description: Sawyer corrects the count when boards are pulled from a pack after counting.

incremental.description: Sawyer keeps the counter lens clean and the label printer stocked.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: half of the lines have no counter and many packs are mixed, so counting and sorting stay mostly by hand (14.4); high: about 70% of lines counted as assumed (21.6).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Get the work order, examine blueprints, drawings, cutting lists or patterns to determine set-up, procedures and final dimensions, work out the saw set-up and ask the supervisor about unclear orders.

steps.what: Sawyer collects the paper work order and cutting list from the office
Sawyer examines the cutting list, drawings or patterns to determine final dimensions
Sawyer works out the cutting sequence for the order
Sawyer works out the set-up: blade spacing, fence and stop settings
Sawyer asks the supervisor about unclear orders

tasks.design: Work orders and cutting lists released by production planning appear on the line terminal at the saw, so nobody walks to the office for paper. On computer-controlled saws the cutting program for the order loads from the work order and the sawyer checks the settings; on manual saws the sawyer works out the set-up as today. Reading drawings and settling questions stay with the sawyer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Orders were on paper at the office and every set-up was worked out by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Line terminals showing work orders, and saw controllers that load programs per order.
tasks.still_hard: Orders with special patterns or poor drawings.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing how a log will open up before cutting.
tasks.altitude: Less walking and set-up arithmetic; reading orders stays with the sawyer.

reach.learn: Whether orders on the terminal cause fewer set-up questions.

evidence.claim: Computer-controlled saws load cutting programs per order from a work order system.
No AI is needed; orders and programs are fixed data.

assumptions: Boundary: preparing a job at the saw; cutting is a separate task.
Input contract for s1: work orders and cutting lists released by production planning in the {ERP} and shown on the line terminal.
Input contract for s4: cutting programs per order prepared by the planner for computer-controlled saws, about 40% of saws; manual saws keep the full set-up; s4 is priced at that share.

Reading drawings and questions keep their full time. s3 keeps 70 and s4 keeps 75 because only on computer-controlled saws, about 40%, the loaded program holds the sequence and settings for the sawyer to check; s1 keeps 30 for orders still on paper.
research_questions: Do set-up errors fall on saws that load programs?

already_counted.description: Sawyer checks loaded settings against the order before the first cut.

incremental.description: Sawyer reports wrong programs to the planner.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: only about a fifth of the saws are computer-controlled and special orders still come on paper (12.3); high: about 40% of saws load programs as assumed (20.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Have packs scanned into the yard, read which stock the order needs, find and select the stock, select saw blades and check them, and choose cutting procedures with the supervisor for awkward stock.

steps.what: Forklift driver scans each pack label when putting it away in the yard
Sawyer reads which types or grades of stock and dimensions the work order needs: worked out from the paper cutting list today, shown on the line terminal after the change
Sawyer finds and selects the right stock in the yard
Sawyer selects saw blades and checks their condition
Sawyer chooses the cutting procedure with the supervisor for awkward stock

tasks.design: The line terminal shows the stock grade and dimensions each order needs and where matching packs are in the yard, from the pack labels the forklift driver scans at put-away. Choosing and checking blades and agreeing cutting procedures for awkward stock stay with the sawyer and supervisor.
tasks.previous_blocker: Stock was searched in the yard by walking the rows.
tasks.enabler_now: Pack labels scanned into yard locations and shown on line terminals.
tasks.still_hard: Stock whose real quality differs from its label.
tasks.human_edge: Choosing the blade that suits today's wood.
tasks.altitude: Less searching; selection judgement stays with the sawyer.

reach.task: Put packs away in the yard
reach.learn: Whether scanning at put-away slows the driver.

evidence.claim: Yard location systems record pack locations from scanned labels.
No AI is used; stock and blade lists are fixed data.

assumptions: Boundary: choosing stock, blades and procedure for an order; sawing is outside.

Input contract for s3: pack locations recorded by the forklift driver scanning labels at put-away (s1), with about the effort of noting the row on paper; packs without labels are searched as today (about 30%).

Blade selection and procedure choice keep their full time; s2 keeps 80 because reading stays and only working the stock out of the cutting list goes; s3 keeps 75 because walking to the pack and selecting stay; driver time is outside the sawyer's savings.
unknowns: Size of the yard and number of stock grades.

incremental.description: Sawyer reports packs that are not where the terminal says.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: half of the packs have no label, so half of the stock is still searched by walking the rows (8.1); high: about 70% of packs labelled as assumed (12.9).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional
